metadata.author: Greg Paskal
metadata.description: Slow HTTP response time finding template with comprehensive guidance for all audiences including framework-specific optimization techniques, database query tuning, async processing patterns, caching strategies, and infrastructure scaling to improve server response times and user experience.

EXECUTIVE.summary: Your application has slow server response times (TTFB > 600ms), directly impacting user experience, conversions, and revenue. Slow responses cause page abandonment, lost sales, and poor search rankings.
EXECUTIVE.businessRisk: Critical risk of revenue loss through poor performance. Studies show 1-second delay reduces conversions by 7%, 2 seconds by 20%, 3+ seconds causes 53% abandonment (Google). Slow responses compound with network latency, causing total page loads of 5-10+ seconds. E-commerce loses $1.6M annually per 100ms delay (Amazon data). Customer satisfaction drops 16% per second of delay. Poor Core Web Vitals (TTFB > 800ms) harm SEO rankings, reducing organic traffic 20-40%. Competitors with faster backends gain market share. High bounce rates damage brand perception. Mobile users particularly affected. Server response time often the largest contributor to total page load time.
EXECUTIVE.complianceImpact: Google Core Web Vitals require TTFB < 800ms (good), < 1800ms (needs improvement). SLA violations if response time SLAs exist. Web Performance Best Practices mandate optimization. Industry standards: TTFB < 200ms (excellent), < 600ms (acceptable), > 1000ms (poor).

PROJECT_MANAGER.summary: Server response times exceed acceptable thresholds (TTFB > 600ms), indicating backend performance issues requiring database optimization, caching implementation, or infrastructure scaling.
PROJECT_MANAGER.timeline: Should be addressed immediately if TTFB > 1000ms. Current sprint if 600-1000ms. Medium complexity - may require database tuning, caching, code optimization, or infrastructure changes. Critical priority for customer-facing applications.
PROJECT_MANAGER.effort: 4-8 hours for initial diagnosis and quick wins (caching, query optimization). 1-2 weeks for comprehensive optimization (database indexing, code refactoring, async processing). Ongoing monitoring and tuning required.
dependencies: Access to application performance monitoring (APM) tools
Infrastructure team for scaling if needed

DEVELOPER.summary: Server response time (Time To First Byte - TTFB) exceeds acceptable thresholds, indicating backend bottlenecks in database queries, business logic, external API calls, or resource constraints.
DEVELOPER.technical: TTFB measures time from request initiation to first byte of response. Components: Network latency (out of control), Server processing time (optimize this), Database query time (often biggest factor), External API calls, CPU/memory constraints. Common causes: N+1 query problems (ORM lazy loading), Missing database indexes, Unoptimized queries (full table scans), Blocking I/O operations, Synchronous external API calls, Inefficient algorithms (O(n²) vs O(n log n)), Memory leaks causing GC pauses, Thread pool exhaustion, Connection pool exhaustion, Cold start issues (serverless), Lack of caching. Optimization strategies: Database query optimization (indexes, query tuning, connection pooling), Caching (Redis, Memcached for database results, API responses), Async processing (message queues for non-critical tasks), Code profiling (identify hot paths), Algorithm optimization, External API timeout/circuit breakers, Horizontal scaling (load balancing), Vertical scaling (more CPU/RAM), CDN for static content offload. Tools: APM (New Relic, DataDog, Dynatrace), Database query analyzers (EXPLAIN, slow query log), Profilers (Java Flight Recorder, Node.js Clinic, Python cProfile).
DEVELOPER.vulnerability: CWE-400 (Uncontrolled Resource Consumption). Slow responses consume server resources longer, reducing capacity and creating DoS vulnerability. Under load, slow endpoints amplify problems causing cascading failures. Not primary security vulnerability but affects availability and resilience.

SECURITY_ENGINEER.summary: Slow response times create availability vulnerability by consuming excessive server resources, reducing capacity for legitimate traffic, and increasing attack surface for resource exhaustion attacks.
SECURITY_ENGINEER.vulnerability: CWE-400 (Uncontrolled Resource Consumption). Slow endpoints consume server resources (threads, connections, memory) for extended periods. Under attack or high load, slow responses amplify impact causing resource exhaustion, thread pool depletion, connection timeouts, and eventual service unavailability. Attackers can exploit slow endpoints to amplify DoS attacks. Particularly vulnerable: endpoints with database queries without indexes, endpoints calling slow external APIs synchronously, endpoints with O(n²) algorithms. Slow responses also mask other issues and make monitoring/alerting less effective.
SECURITY_ENGINEER.attackVector: Attacker identifies slow endpoints through reconnaissance. Sends moderate traffic targeting slow endpoints to exhaust server resources. Each request holds resources much longer than fast endpoints. Thread pools deplete, new requests queue or timeout. Database connection pools exhaust. Application becomes unresponsive to all users. Not high-severity direct exploit but contributes to overall availability posture. Combined with other vulnerabilities creates cascading failures.
SECURITY_ENGINEER.threatLevel: MEDIUM - Primarily availability concern with security implications. Main risk is degraded availability under load or attack rather than direct exploit. However, critical for system resilience and defense-in-depth. Slow endpoints are force multipliers for DoS attacks. Fix improves both performance and security posture.
SECURITY_ENGINEER.mitigationUrgency: Immediate if TTFB > 2000ms (critical). Within 1 week if > 1000ms (high). Within 2 weeks if > 600ms (medium). Medium complexity requiring systematic analysis. Higher priority if: public-facing APIs, high-traffic endpoints, endpoints handling payments/transactions, applications with SLAs, or identified as DoS risk.

OPS_INFRASTRUCTURE.summary: Application servers returning slow responses indicate backend resource constraints, database bottlenecks, or architectural issues requiring performance tuning, caching, or infrastructure scaling.
OPS_INFRASTRUCTURE.technical: Slow TTFB indicates backend processing delays. Investigate: Application servers (CPU usage > 70%, memory pressure, GC pauses), Database (slow queries, missing indexes, connection pool exhaustion), Network (high latency to dependencies, DNS issues), External services (third-party API delays). Monitoring metrics: TTFB (target < 200ms excellent, < 600ms acceptable), P50/P95/P99 response times, Database query time, External API call time, CPU/Memory utilization, Thread pool metrics, Connection pool metrics, Error rates. Optimization approaches: Horizontal scaling (add more servers, load balance), Vertical scaling (larger instances), Database optimization (read replicas, sharding), Caching layer (Redis/Memcached), CDN for static content, Async processing (queues for background tasks), Connection pooling tuning, Database connection limits. Infrastructure as Code: Auto-scaling based on metrics, Load balancer configuration, Health checks, Circuit breakers for external dependencies.
OPS_INFRASTRUCTURE.scope: All application servers, databases, load balancers, and external service dependencies. Affects user-facing endpoints most critically. Consider: Geographic distribution (multi-region), Database replication lag, Cache hit rates, Queue depths. Must optimize across full stack: Frontend (already fast but waiting on backend), Backend API servers, Databases, External services, Network infrastructure.
OPS_INFRASTRUCTURE.monitoring: Monitor comprehensive metrics: TTFB (P50/P95/P99), Response time breakdown (DB time, API time, business logic), Error rates (timeouts, 500s), Infrastructure metrics (CPU, memory, disk I/O, network), Database metrics (query time, connections, locks), Cache metrics (hit rate, evictions), Queue metrics (depth, processing time). Set alerts: TTFB P95 > 1000ms (warning), > 2000ms (critical), Error rate > 1% (warning), > 5% (critical), CPU > 80% (warning), Database connections > 80% capacity (warning). Use APM tools for distributed tracing.

QA_TESTER.summary: Slow server response times prevent validation of performance requirements and indicate need for load testing to identify bottlenecks and capacity limits.
QA_TESTER.testImplication: Cannot validate performance SLAs with slow TTFB. Performance testing shows unacceptable response times under load. Need to: Establish baseline response times, Identify slow endpoints, Conduct load testing to find breaking points, Profile application under load, Test different user scenarios, Measure impact of optimizations. Tools: Apache JMeter, k6, Gatling, Locust for load testing. Browser DevTools for TTFB measurement. APM tools for production monitoring.
QA_TESTER.riskIfNotFixed: Failed performance testing. SLA violations. Poor user experience metrics. Customer complaints. High abandonment rates. Failed capacity planning. Production incidents under load. Inability to scale. Poor Core Web Vitals scores. SEO ranking penalties. Revenue loss from slow checkouts. Competitive disadvantage.

generic.code:
# Response Time Optimization Checklist

## 1. Database Optimization
- Add indexes on frequently queried columns
- Optimize slow queries (use EXPLAIN)
- Fix N+1 query problems
- Use connection pooling
- Consider read replicas for read-heavy loads

## 2. Caching Strategy
- Implement Redis/Memcached for frequently accessed data
- Cache database query results
- Cache API responses
- Use CDN for static assets
- Browser caching for repeat visits

## 3. Async Processing
- Move non-critical tasks to background queues
- Use async/await for I/O operations
- Don't block requests waiting for emails, notifications, etc.
- Parallel processing where possible

## 4. Code Optimization
- Profile code to find hot paths
- Optimize algorithms (O(n²) → O(n log n))
- Reduce unnecessary computations
- Lazy load data when possible
- Use pagination for large datasets

## 5. External API Calls
- Set timeouts (5-10 seconds max)
- Use circuit breakers for failing services
- Cache external API responses
- Call external APIs asynchronously
- Have fallback mechanisms

## 6. Infrastructure
- Horizontal scaling (more servers)
- Vertical scaling (larger instances)
- Load balancing
- Auto-scaling based on metrics
- Regional distribution

# Target: time_starttransfer < 0.6s

monitoring.config:
# Application Performance Monitoring Setup

## New Relic APM
newrelic:
  app_name: 'MyApp Production'
  license_key: 'YOUR_LICENSE_KEY'
  log_level: 'info'
  transaction_tracer:
    enabled: true
    transaction_threshold: apdex_f
    record_sql: obfuscated
  error_collector:
    enabled: true

## DataDog APM
DD_AGENT_HOST: 'datadog-agent'
DD_TRACE_ENABLED: true
DD_SERVICE: 'myapp'
DD_ENV: 'production'

## Prometheus + Grafana
# Track response time metrics
http_request_duration_seconds:
  type: histogram
  help: 'HTTP request duration'
  buckets: [0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 5.0]

## Database Slow Query Log
# MySQL
SET GLOBAL slow_query_log = 'ON';
SET GLOBAL long_query_time = 1;  # Log queries > 1 second
SET GLOBAL slow_query_log_file = '/var/log/mysql/slow.log';

# PostgreSQL (postgresql.conf)
log_min_duration_statement = 1000  # Log queries > 1 second
monitoring.reload:
# Restart application with monitoring enabled
systemctl restart myapp

# Verify monitoring agent running
systemctl status newrelic-infra
monitoring.verify:
# Check metrics are being collected
curl http://localhost:9090/metrics  # Prometheus

# View APM dashboard
# NewRelic: https://one.newrelic.com
# DataDog: https://app.datadoghq.com

database.config:
# Database Performance Tuning

## PostgreSQL
# postgresql.conf
shared_buffers = 4GB              # 25% of RAM
effective_cache_size = 12GB       # 75% of RAM
work_mem = 64MB
maintenance_work_mem = 1GB
max_connections = 200
random_page_cost = 1.1            # For SSD

# Enable query performance monitoring
shared_preload_libraries = 'pg_stat_statements'
pg_stat_statements.track = all

## MySQL
# my.cnf
innodb_buffer_pool_size = 4G      # 70% of RAM
innodb_log_file_size = 512M
max_connections = 200
query_cache_size = 128M
query_cache_limit = 2M
slow_query_log = 1
long_query_time = 1

## Add Indexes
# Find missing indexes
SELECT schemaname, tablename, attname
FROM pg_stats
WHERE schemaname NOT IN ('pg_catalog', 'information_schema')
  AND n_distinct < 0.1
ORDER BY n_distinct;

# Add index example
CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users(email);
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_date ON orders(user_id, created_at);
database.reload:
# PostgreSQL
sudo systemctl reload postgresql

# MySQL
sudo systemctl reload mysql
database.verify:
# Check slow queries
SELECT * FROM pg_stat_statements
ORDER BY mean_time DESC
LIMIT 10;

# Check index usage
SELECT schemaname, tablename, indexname, idx_scan
FROM pg_stat_user_indexes
ORDER BY idx_scan ASC;

autoscaling.config:
# AWS Auto Scaling Configuration

## EC2 Auto Scaling Group
aws autoscaling create-auto-scaling-group \
  --auto-scaling-group-name myapp-asg \
  --launch-configuration-name myapp-lc \
  --min-size 2 \
  --max-size 10 \
  --desired-capacity 4 \
  --target-group-arns arn:aws:elasticloadbalancing:... \
  --health-check-type ELB \
  --health-check-grace-period 300

## Target Tracking Policy (Scale on CPU)
aws autoscaling put-scaling-policy \
  --auto-scaling-group-name myapp-asg \
  --policy-name cpu-target-tracking \
  --policy-type TargetTrackingScaling \
  --target-tracking-configuration '{
    "PredefinedMetricSpecification": {
      "PredefinedMetricType": "ASGAverageCPUUtilization"
    },
    "TargetValue": 70.0
  }'

## Kubernetes HPA
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: myapp-hpa
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: myapp
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 10
  metrics:
  - type: Resource
    resource:
      name: cpu
      target:
        type: Utilization
        averageUtilization: 70
  - type: Resource
    resource:
      name: memory
      target:
        type: Utilization
        averageUtilization: 80
autoscaling.reload:
# Auto scaling updates automatically
# Verify policy
aws autoscaling describe-policies \
  --auto-scaling-group-name myapp-asg
autoscaling.verify:
# Monitor scaling activities
aws autoscaling describe-scaling-activities \
  --auto-scaling-group-name myapp-asg \
  --max-records 10

# Kubernetes
kubectl get hpa
kubectl describe hpa myapp-hpa

OPS_INFRASTRUCTURE.rollbackPlan:
1. Keep baseline performance metrics before changes
2. Implement changes incrementally
3. Monitor each change for impact
4. If performance degrades:
   - Revert recent code deployments
   - Restore previous database configuration
   - Check for resource exhaustion (CPU, memory, connections)
   - Review recent traffic spikes
5. Scale horizontally as temporary fix
6. Analyze root cause before re-implementing
7. Load test in staging before production
